overview:
Moses tells Israel that when the LORD brings them into the land, they are to destroy the seven nations living there, make no covenant or marriages with them, and break down their altars, images, and groves. The reason is Israel's holiness: the LORD chose them as his special people. Obedience will bring blessing on womb, field, and flock, and freedom from the diseases of Egypt. Israel need not fear nations stronger than itself. The LORD who struck Egypt will send the hornet and drive them out little by little, and the images of their gods must be burned, with none of their silver or gold kept.

Verse 7 removes any pride in being chosen. Israel was “the fewest of all people,” and the only causes Moses gives are the LORD's love and the oath he swore to the fathers (v. 8).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Presented as Moses' speeches; the book says Moses wrote “this law” (31:9) and narrates his death. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars connect its core with the law book found under Josiah (2 Kings 22).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its core to the 7th century BC, with additions in the 6th.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The fortieth year after the Exodus (1:3), about 1406 BC by reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The plains of Moab, looking ahead to the conquest of Canaan west of the Jordan.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 23:23–33 and 34:11–16 (no covenant with the nations, the hornet, little by little); Joshua 24:12 (the hornet remembered).

hermeneutics:
Verse 13 promises blessing on “the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep.” The Hebrew words are *sheger* and *ashterot*, and both are also names of deities. A plaster inscription from Deir Alla in the Jordan valley, from about 800 BC, names a goddess pair called Shagar-and-Ashtar, and Ashtart, or Astarte, was a great goddess of Canaan. In the land Israel was entering, the births of the herds could be credited to such powers. Deuteronomy uses their names as plain farm words and puts the fertility of the flocks in the LORD's hands.

When Assyrian armies took a city, they often carried off its gods. Palace reliefs show soldiers bearing statues of conquered gods on their shoulders, and Assyrian kings boast of removing them to Assyria as trophies or hostages. Such statues were wood or stone overlaid with silver and gold, precious booty in their own right. Verse 25 forbids the same profit: Israel must burn the images and may not covet or take the metal on them, “for it is an abomination.” The gods of the land were not to be kept, even as prizes.

Two small silver scrolls found in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, from about 600 BC, were rolled up as amulets. One carries the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26. The other has lines close to v. 9: God keeps covenant and mercy with those who love him and keep his commandments. The confession of this chapter was already being written down and carried in Judah before the exile.

structure.summary: An inclusio: the command to burn the images (v. 5) returns at the end (v. 25), framing the reasons and promises between.

open.text: Destroy the nations; burn their graven images with fire

close.text: The graven images shall ye burn with fire

notes: **Devoted:** the verb *haram*, “utterly destroy,” comes twice in v. 2, an emphatic doubled form, and the noun *herem*, “a cursed thing,” twice in v. 26. The chapter that opens with the nations devoted to destruction ends by warning that an Israelite who brings an idol home becomes devoted like it.
**Love and oath:** the LORD's love is named in vv. 7, 8, and 13, and the oath he “sware” to the fathers in vv. 8, 12, and 13.
**The LORD thy God:** the divine name YHWH occurs 20 times in 26 verses; the conquest is his act from first verse to last.

Chapter 7 sits in the middle of the sermon of chapters 6–8 on the first commandment. Chapter 6 warns against “the gods of the people which are round about you” (6:14); chapter 7 applies that warning to the nations of Canaan; chapter 8 turns to the danger inside Israel, a full stomach and a proud heart.

**Backward and forward:** the list of nations, the hornet, and the slow conquest come from Exodus 23:23–33. Solomon broke v. 3, and 1 Kings 11:2 quotes its warning that foreign wives “will turn away your heart after their gods.”

traditions.text: When his brothers claim the people of Jerusalem are righteous, Nephi asks whether the nations driven out of Canaan were righteous, and answers no. Had they been righteous, he says, Israel would not have been more choice than they, for “the Lord esteemeth all flesh in one,” and he that is righteous is favored of God. Those nations were ripe in iniquity, so the land was cursed to them and blessed to Israel. The Church's footnote to v. 10 points to this passage, which, like vv. 7–8, refuses to make the conquest a reward for Israel's superiority.

After the return from exile, Judah's leaders apply vv. 1–3 to their own day. The princes report to Ezra that the people have not separated from the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and others, and have taken their daughters as wives. Nehemiah makes men swear not to give their daughters to foreign sons or take foreign daughters, in the wording of v. 3, and points to Solomon, whom foreign wives led into sin. The returned community read the old list of Canaanite peoples as a warning about the neighbors of their own time.

Philo paraphrases v. 3 as a command not to marry anyone of another nation, and takes his reason from v. 4. A spouse from outside, he says, may draw children into foreign customs until they forget the honor due to the one God. He adds that even children trained from youth in the sacred laws give their parents real cause for fear. In his reading the ban protects the household's worship of the one God, which is the concern of v. 4.

In his version of Moses' farewell, Josephus has Moses warn that if the laws are broken Israel will be scattered as slaves over sea and land. To keep the laws, he advises, they must leave none of their enemies alive, “lest if you permit them to live, you taste of their manners.” They are also to overthrow the altars and groves and burn all such things with fire. Josephus gives the danger to Israel's way of life as the reason, as v. 4 does.

The Talmud reads v. 3 as making a marriage with a non-Jew legally void, and v. 4 as the source for the rule that a child's status follows the mother. Rabbi Yohanan, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, notes that the verse fears that the foreign husband will turn away “thy son”: the child of your daughter is still called your son. A gentile mother's child, by contrast, is called her son and not yours.

The words “nor shew mercy unto them” (v. 2) are read three ways from the Hebrew spelling: do not praise them, do not give them free gifts, and do not give them a foothold to settle in the land. On v. 25 the rabbis notice a tension: the verse forbids coveting the silver on an idol, yet goes on to speak of taking it. Their answer is that once its gentile owner annuls the image as a god, the metal may be used.

Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yose the Galilean reads v. 7 against its plain sense: God says he loves Israel because, when he gives them greatness, they make themselves small. Rashi, quoting him, lists Abraham's “which am but dust and ashes” and Moses and Aaron's “what are we?” against the boasts of Nebuchadnezzar, Sennacherib, and Hiram of Tyre. Rashi first notes the plain meaning: Israel really was the smallest people.

The Greek of v. 6 calls Israel a *laos periousios*, a “peculiar people,” the LORD's own possession. Titus 2:14 uses the phrase for those Christ redeems and purifies, and 1 Peter 2:9 joins it to the titles of Exodus 19:6 for the church: “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation.” The language of vv. 6–8 is carried over to the Christian community.

A monk of southern Gaul, Cassian reads the seven nations of v. 1 as the soul's chief vices, which are “greater and mightier” than the monk himself. Egypt, already left behind, stands for gluttony, making eight in all. The promise that the LORD will drive them out “by little and little” (v. 22) becomes a rule of spiritual struggle: fight one vice at a time and trust God for the victory. He quotes 8:12–15 against pride once a vice is beaten.
